I think the phenomenon you're describing is a result of:

  • "Low hanging fruit"/Lowest-common-denominator content
  • Instant gratification == Instant upvotes (i.e. on reddit)
  • Mass quantities of users == Userbase more similar to "average" population (via LoLN)

So memes rocket to the top because statistically speaking, most people are "average" (read: have a normal level of expertise for a subverse as opposed to insightful discussion to contribute) and will upvoate a half-second meme.

Another key part of this machine is the one-user-one-vote rule, which some have argued can be optimized---namely, to give "better" users (content curators?) more sway over the journey of a poast.

I think one of the best things voat could do, is stay away from the idea of 'default subverses' -- don't automatically subscribe people to subverses, let them pick and choose their content.

This prevents popular subverses from turning into cesspools, much like r/atheism.

Before it became a default it was mostly about discussions and relevant politics.

When it became a default subreddit, it devolved into a constant stream of 5-second memes.

After it got removed as a default subreddit, the mods changed the rules and the content became much more tolerable again.

Forcing people to pick the groups they choose to become a part of, lessens the chances of people who don't actually care for the groups original content, joining it.

I'm looking forward to Voat growing a bit larger or at least having a more active community. At the moment, because so few people can downvote incorrect/misleading content, a lot of dubious stuff is making its way to the front page. Since the policy is limited moderation from mods, I think we need more active users (whether that means more users or the users we have becoming more active) to self-moderate. Essentially, I suspect that if we have more users incoming, the ratio of lurkers/users will stay about the same, which just means a small portion of new active users. Even on reddit, it was clear that there were voices louder than others, even with the volume of users. Users that were most visible were the ones posting a lot (which were often karma farmers and self-promoters) or the ones that exclusively browsed new posts of popular subs. By the time anything hit the front page on larger subs, you could post, but never be seen. In essence, it's not just about being drowned out by the volume of users, but also making sure to contribute to posts when they're new that really gets your voice heard.

Basically, there is a signal to noise graph; which means, that, with more signals (users) transmitting (commenting, posting), the harder it is to find a legitimate signal (post or comment), that is relevant to the person. Smaller subverses obviously have this signal to noise ratio lower, as there are less signals to filter through.
That is a traditional problem with reddit; as long as Voat doesn't try to be reddit, and develop on it's own, there are multiple ways to distribute the voices across subverses evenly I think.
